chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Muhammad ibn Khalid from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) about a man who deposited with another man wealth that had value, and the man who held the wealth was an Arab who was able to give him nothing and was unable to be compelled to give him anything, and the man who deposited it with him was a 'khariji' (expendable/liable), so I did not leave out anything. He said to me, 'Tell him to return his wealth to him, for he entrusted it to him with the trust of Allah, Exalted and Glorious.' I said, 'And a man bought from a woman of the Abbasids some of their plots, and wrote for her a document stating that she had received the money, but she had not received it; should he give her the money or withhold it?' He said to me, 'Tell him to withhold it from her with the strongest withholding, for she sold what she did not possess.'

key_terms.بَاعَتْهُ مَا لَمْ تَمْلِكْهُ: she sold what she did not possess
key_terms.خَارِجِيٌّ: Khariji (a specific group or one liable for payment)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on returning a deposited wealth to a debtor who cannot easily be compelled to pay?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between general debt and specific deposited wealth (*amanah*), ruling that the latter must be returned regardless of the debtor's ability to pay, as it is held in God's trust. It further illustrates the principle of *gharar* (uncertainty) or lack of possession in sales, where a buyer withholds payment if the seller has not yet acquired the goods, preventing the sale of what one does not own. These rulings highlight the Shia juristic emphasis on the sanctity of trust (*amanah*) and the conditions of valid transfer of ownership (*milkiyah*).
